analysis.one_liner: Cuts the capital gains tax rate to 15 percent and lets investors adjust asset costs for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 1989 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change two things about how capital gains are taxed. First, when someone sells corporate stock or business property they have held for more than a year, the purchase cost would be adjusted upward for inflation, so taxes would apply only to gains above the rise in the general price level [S3]. Second, it would cut the special tax rate on capital gains to a flat 15 percent, down from the 34 percent corporate rate and the ordinary income rates that applied to individuals after the 1986 tax overhaul [S2]. It was introduced by a Republican congressman on the first day of the 101st Congress and sent to the tax-writing committee, which took no action on it [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Investors who sell corporate stock and business property for more than they paid. Indexing for inflation shields them from being taxed on gains that merely match price increases, and the 15 percent rate would sharply lower taxes on realized gains [S2]. Because large capital gains are concentrated among higher-income households and corporations, the biggest dollar benefits would flow to those groups; small savers holding stock through mutual funds would also get some protection from inflation [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Sellers of corporate stock and long-held business property could increase the cost basis of their assets by the rise in the gross national product deflator, so they would owe tax only on gains above inflation [S3].
The bill sets a flat 15 percent alternative tax rate on net capital gains, replacing the 34 percent rate that applied to corporations after the 1986 reform [S2].
It lowers the minimum tax on capital gains as well, so taxpayers cannot end up paying more through the alternative minimum tax [S3].

Mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, and partnerships would pass the indexing adjustment through to their shareholders and partners, extending the benefit to small investors who hold assets through pooled vehicles [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less revenue, since both the rate cut and inflation indexing reduce the tax on gains, and that lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers or by borrowing [S2]. After the 1986 tax reform, Congress had deliberately taxed capital gains at the same rates as wages to keep the code simple and prevent high earners from converting income into lightly taxed gains; this bill reverses that choice for stock and business assets [S2].

drawbacks.text: Cutting the capital gains rate to 15 percent while wages are taxed at higher rates gives investors a lower rate than workers, and the biggest dollar savings go to those with the largest gains [S2].

Inflation indexing applies only to corporate stock and business property, not to ordinary savings accounts or wages, so the inflation relief in the bill flows to asset holders rather than to people whose pay is eroded by inflation [S3].
Both provisions reduce federal revenue, which under the budget rules of the era would have had to be offset by other tax increases or spending cuts [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Protecting savers from being taxed on inflation rather than real gain is a defensible idea, but this bill pairs it with a steep rate cut that mainly benefits large investors and corporations. The modest inflation protection for small stockholders is outweighed by the revenue loss and by the advantage the 15 percent rate creates over the taxation of wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John J. Rhodes III of Arizona introduced the bill on January 4, 1989, the opening day of the 101st Congress, joined by two original cosponsors [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which writes tax legislation [S5].
Fifteen House Republicans had signed on as cosponsors; no Democrats did [S4].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it died at the end of the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991, without ever reaching the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new tax break, so the 1986 settlement that taxed capital gains like ordinary income stayed in place; supporters of the rate cut walked away with nothing.

for.name: Rep. John J. Rhodes III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to index asset basis for inflation and cap the capital gains rate at 15 percent.

for.name: 15 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 4, 1989 and never reported it out, holding no hearing or vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the Democratic-controlled Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The 15 percent rate and inflation indexing would cut taxes most for those with the largest gains in stock and business property, a group concentrated at the top of the income scale; the revenue given up would be borne by other taxpayers [S2][S3].
The corporate capital gains rate would drop from 34 percent to 15 percent, cutting tax bills on corporate asset sales [S2].

industries.industry: Mutual funds and real estate investment trusts
industries.note: The bill lets these pooled vehicles pass inflation indexing through to their investors, extending some of the benefit to ordinary small savers [S3].
Both provisions reduce tax collected on gains, shrinking federal revenue that funds services for everyone [S2].
